vignette:
He is 54, a Middle Eastern man who has spent most of his adult life working as a software engineer, someone who once took comfort in systems that behaved predictably. He lives alone now and has for many years. In conversation he is careful, precise, and polite, the kind of person who chooses words the way other people debug code. It takes several sessions before he tells the story directly, and even then he does so in fragments, circling around it before he can stay with it.

The assault happens when he is in his late twenties, newly settled in the United States and still trying to find his footing professionally and socially. He is bright, ambitious, and lonely in a way he does not name at the time. He is working long hours at his first serious engineering job, eager to prove himself, speaking to his family back home only occasionally because of the time difference and because he does not want them to hear how isolated he feels. One evening, after a work-related social outing, a man he knows casually offers him a ride. He accepts. What follows is something he still struggles to describe without going blank. He remembers the smell in the car, the pressure of a hand, the sudden certainty that he is no longer in control of what is happening. He remembers freezing. He remembers trying to calculate how to get out safely, as if there might be a logical sequence that would undo what is already underway. Afterward, he feels split off from himself, watching his own body move through the rest of the night as though it belongs to someone else.

In the days that follow, he goes to work as usual. He writes code, attends meetings, answers questions. From the outside, nothing appears different. Inside, he is flooded by shame. He tells no one. Part of the silence comes from fear that he will not be believed; part comes from the cultural world he carries with him, where masculinity, privacy, and honor feel tightly bound together. He cannot imagine saying the words aloud. He begins to think of the assault as evidence of some failure in him rather than as something done to him. He showers compulsively. He throws away the clothes he had been wearing. At night he lies awake replaying isolated moments-the turn of the car, the sound of the door locks, his own body not fighting in the way he thinks it should have. He comes to hate that memory most of all, the paralysis, which he misreads as consent.

Sleep becomes fractured almost immediately. When he does sleep, he has vivid dreams that leave him waking with his heart racing and his shirt damp with sweat. Sometimes the dreams are exact; more often they are distorted but carry the same helplessness. During the day, he startles at sudden movement and feels a jolt of panic when someone stands too close behind him. He starts taking stairs instead of elevators if he is alone with another man. He avoids social gatherings after work and tells colleagues he is busy. His world narrows with very little conscious decision. He begins organizing his life around not feeling exposed.

Over the years he becomes highly successful in his field. He is known as dependable, technically gifted, and unusually calm under pressure. Work suits him because it rewards vigilance and control. He can spend hours tracing an error through layers of a system and feel, briefly, competent again. But the same habits harden into isolation. He avoids dating entirely. When friends try to set him up, he laughs it off or says he is married to his job. Physical closeness feels dangerous, and even casual touch can make his stomach clench. On crowded public transportation he positions himself near exits and scans faces without realizing he is doing it. In parking garages he grips his keys between his fingers and checks the back seat of his car before getting in.

There are periods when he tells himself he has moved on. Then something small-a cologne similar to the one he remembers, a scene in a television show, a younger coworker jokingly blocking a doorway-drops him back into the original terror with humiliating speed. In those moments he is no longer a middle-aged engineer in an office; he is in the car again, trapped, his mind going white around the edges. He becomes skilled at disguising these episodes. He mutes his microphone during remote meetings to steady his breathing. He excuses himself from conference rooms and stands in the restroom until the shaking passes.

What pains him now is not only the memory of the assault but the life that has formed around it. He describes himself as living "defensively," as though every choice must first be run through a threat model. He keeps his apartment sparse and orderly. He double-checks locks, avoids visitors, and sleeps lightly, waking at minor noises. He feels detached from other people, especially when they speak easily about intimacy or trust. He often assumes hidden motives where none exist, then feels guilty and exhausted by his own suspicion.

By the time he speaks about the assault in therapy, he has carried it alone for more than two decades. He says the secrecy has become its own prison. Even while telling it, he watches for signs of judgment. He apologizes for being indirect. Yet beneath the restraint there is grief-for the younger man who was harmed, for the years shaped by fear, and for how thoroughly one night taught him that his body and the world were no longer safe.
